title: Rejoice always (Philippians 4:4–7)
hook: be nothing solicitous, and the peace of God keeps your hearts

segments.voice: Yesterday, forgetting the things that are behind, and pressing towards the mark. Your line was press on. Which way were you facing? Day five hundred eighty-nine.

Once a year in Advent, many Catholic priests set aside the purple and wear rose. On the wreath, the pink candle is lit. That Sunday has a name, Gaudete, the Latin for rejoice, from the first word of the old entrance chant. And the chant is today's verse: Gaudete in Domino semper, rejoice in the Lord always. The surprising part is where Paul was when he wrote it. Not on a holiday. In prison, not knowing whether he'd live or die.
screen: `ROSE VESTMENTS IN ADVENT.` → `GAUDETE: REJOICE.` → `WRITTEN FROM PRISON.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "Rejoice in the Lord always; again, I say, rejoice. Let your modesty be known to all men. The Lord is nigh." He says it twice, as if he expects them to hesitate. Modesty here translates a Greek word that means something like gentleness or graciousness, not grabbing what's yours. Then: the Lord is nigh. Near. Near in time, coming soon? Or near in space, right beside you? Readers have taken it both ways, and the verse can hold both. Then comes the instruction: "Be nothing solicitous; but in every thing, by prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your petitions be made known to God." Be nothing solicitous is old English for don't be anxious about anything. And notice what Paul doesn't say. He doesn't say stop worrying because there's nothing to worry about. He says take the worry and turn it into a request, with thanks attached. Then the promise: "And the peace of God, which surpasseth all understanding, keep your hearts and minds in Christ Jesus." The Greek for keep is a soldier's word: to guard, to garrison. Philippi was a Roman colony, settled by veterans, and its people knew what a garrison looked like. Paul pictures God's peace standing guard at the gate of your heart. Not peace that understands everything. Peace that surpasses understanding: it holds even when the situation doesn't make sense. On Gaudete Sunday, the Church is still waiting for Christmas. The rejoicing comes before the gifts are open.
screen: `REJOICE, AND AGAIN: REJOICE.` · `THE LORD IS NEAR: TIME, OR PLACE?` · `TURN THE WORRY INTO A REQUEST.` · `PEACE STANDING GUARD.` · then, large: `THE PEACE OF GOD, WHICH SURPASSETH ALL UNDERSTANDING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: turn one worry around. Settle, and breathe. Let one worry come to the front of your mind, the one that's loudest today. Name it plainly. Now, instead of chewing on it, shape it into a request: help with this, or watch over them, or show me the next step. Then add one thing you're thankful for, right next to it. If you pray, you can make it known to God, just as it is. If you don't, simply set it down in words and notice whether anything loosens. The bell holds the time.
Rejoice always. Paul's words from prison, sung every Gaudete Sunday: rejoice in the Lord always, for the Lord is nigh. Today's word.
Your line: the lord is nigh. Today, when a worry flares, turn it into a request, add one thanks, and leave it there. Day five hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: On the Third Sunday of Advent, Gaudete Sunday, Catholics light the rose candle on the Advent wreath, priests may wear rose vestments, and the entrance antiphon is taken from Philippians 4:4–5.

notes: Gaudete Sunday: entrance antiphon 'Gaudete in Domino semper' (Phil 4:4–5); rose vestments optional. Confirm.
Greek epieikes ('modesty' in DR) as gentleness/graciousness. Confirm.
phroureō as a military term, and Philippi as a Roman colony settled by veterans: standard commentary. Confirm.
Paul's imprisonment while writing Philippians (1:13, 1:20–24); location debated (Rome, Ephesus, Caesarea) and not specified here.
